literature: activation function, ungrokk.summary: Q1: No paper ties ungrokking to the activation function. Varma et al. (arXiv 2309.02390) explain ungrokking by circuit efficiency under weight decay and a critical training-set size D_crit; the activation enters their theory only through a homogeneity exponent kappa and is never varied; most of their runs had no slingshots. The only activation-specific loss of generalisation found is a single-run observation with an x^3 activation in a 2-layer MLP (arXiv 2411.05353), and a 2026 test-time swap (arXiv 2602.16849) shows that a modular-addition ReLU network relies on the even part of its activation (|x|, x^2 work equally; x, x^3 fail). Q2: grokking needs no particular activation and no nonlinearity at all (linear estimators, logistic regression, Gaussian processes, kernel machines with AGOP); the one controlled activation comparison (arXiv 2603.25009, March 2026) finds GELU 4.3x faster than ReLU in one regime and failing in another. Q3: periodic late-training spikes with norm growth are documented in exactly the toy's setup (Thilak et al.: 2-layer transformer, division mod 97, Adam lr 1e-3, betas 0.9/0.98, eps 1e-8, batch 512), also with weight decay 0.1 to 1.0 (Thilak App. C.1; Nanda et al. App. D.2) and in a 6-layer linear network. A NeurIPS 2026 paper (arXiv 2605.06152) traces them to float32 absorption in the cross-entropy (softmax collapse) amplified by Adam's maximal step eta/eps; casting only the logits/loss to float64 removed them. Larger eps (1e-5) removes them in three papers but slows or stops learning; a 3x smaller learning rate is, by the same accounts, expected to delay rather than remove them. Q4: degree-2 (bilinear) GLUs come close to SwiGLU in language-model loss (Shazeer 1.648 vs 1.636; Pearce et al. 1.337 vs 1.321; TinyLlama converted by fine-tuning at about +0.05 loss), but no paper measures how much of a trained SwiGLU layer's output a degree-2 approximation captures (the >95% figure of Belrose and Rigg is for a ReLU MLP on MNIST-like inputs). Checked identity: silu(g) = g/2 + (g/2) tanh(g/2), so the input-even part of every SwiGLU unit is exactly g*u/2. Q5: the multiplication constructions are confirmed (Lin-Tegmark-Rolnick 4-neuron gate is the polarisation identity via the even part of a smooth activation; Yarotsky uses xy = ((x+y)^2 - x^2 - y^2)/2 with sawtooth squaring). The neural feature ansatz is stated for every layer, but for the weights, with gradients taken with respect to that layer's own input and of the trained network; only the first-layer case equals an expected gradient outer product. The project's last-layer/target finding is therefore not an instance of it; it connects only through the first layer. Q6: 15 web searches (listed in the Q6 item); 2025-2026 additions are in the items; none links ungrokking to the activation.

items.question: Q1
items.claim: Varma et al. attribute ungrokking to circuit efficiency under weight decay: below a critical training-set size D_crit the memorising circuit is the more efficient one, and continued training moves weight to it. The activation function is never varied; it enters only their toy model, through an exponent kappa.
items.citation: Varma, Shah, Kenton, Kramar, Kumar (2023), 'Explaining grokking through circuit efficiency', arXiv 2309.02390 v1.
items.how_read: Full text (HTML text copy from the project's earlier review, <S>/kv_review/scout_lit/txt/2309.02390_html.txt). Re-read for this question: Sections 3 to 7, Appendix A (A.1, A.2), D.1 and Theorem D.4; whole text searched for activation, ReLU, GELU, nonlinear, quadratic, slingshot.
items.finding: Section 4.2: after grokking, training on D' < D_crit makes 'C_mem ... now more efficient than C_gen, and so we predict that with enough further training gradient descent will reallocate weight from C_gen to C_mem'. Measured (Sec. 5.2, Fig. 4, Fig. 8): final test accuracy against reduced dataset size shows a sharp transition near D_crit, independent of weight-decay strength; examples are only removed; called 'a special case of catastrophic forgetting'. Setup (App. A): 1-layer transformer, d_model 128, 4 heads, d_mlp 512, full-batch AdamW, betas 0.9/0.98, lr 1e-3, weight decay 1.0, a+b mod 113 plus 9 further tasks; the MLP activation is not stated (Nanda et al. 2023, whose architecture this is, call theirs 'a one-layer ReLU transformer'). The only mention of an activation: 'In a kappa-layer MLP with Relu activations and without biases, scaling all parameters by a constant c scales the outputs by c^kappa', used to model a circuit's parameter norm as w^(1/kappa) P. Theorem D.4 (L_q weight decay): if kappa >= q all weight goes to the most efficient circuit(s); if 0 < kappa < q the weights are proportional to P_i^(-q kappa/(q - kappa)), a mixture. Sec. 6: 'our explanation applies even where there are no slingshots or oscillations (as in most of our experiments)'.
items.bears_on: S1 (against the strong form 'in the end the activation function'), E1, E3. The published cause is training-set size relative to D_crit, with weight decay. In this framework an activation could matter only through kappa (how logits scale with parameter scale) or through which circuits are learnable. My inference, not in the paper: with a layer norm after every sub-block, as in the toy, the logit scale is set by the last norm gain and the unembedding, so swapping the MLP nonlinearity need not change kappa. Varma's ungrokking happened mostly without slingshots, so E3's question (does the toy's ungrokking need its collapses?) is a fair one.

items.question: Q1, Q2
items.claim: The only primary source found in which generalisation is lost under continued training because of the activation function: with activation x^3 the test accuracy of a 2-layer MLP on modular addition rises to a maximum and then decreases, while with |x^3| it stays at the maximum. Odd activations do not grok; adding an odd term x to x^2 delays grokking.
items.citation: Salah, Yevick (2024), 'Controlling Grokking with Nonlinearity and Data Symmetry', arXiv 2411.05353 v1 (8 Nov 2024; no journal reference listed).
items.how_read: Full text (PDF converted to text).
items.finding: Model: 2-layer MLP without embeddings, two concatenated one-hot inputs, a+b mod P, cross-entropy, Adam with weight decay. Section 3.2: for activations x + a x^2, 'for P=27 and TRAIN_FRAC = 0.8, the number of epochs before grokking occurs decreases as the value of a increases. Evidently, the odd, x, term delays the rise of the test accuracy ... Grokking also does not occur for odd activation functions x^2 sign(x) and x^3. In the latter case the test accuracy rises to a maximum value before decreasing, as evident in Fig. 7. In contrast, for a |x^3| activation function, the test accuracy rises and then remains at a maximum value. Taken together, these results establish that a rapid onset of grokking requires that the activation function be even and that the onset of grokking can be delayed an arbitrary number of epochs by incorporating an odd, non-grokking component'. Also (P = 20, 70% training data): 'the test accuracy decreases after reaching 1' (no activation dependence stated). Seeds, learning rate and number of runs are not reported; the curves appear to be single runs.
items.bears_on: S1, S3, E1. Weak but direct evidence that the activation can decide whether generalisation is kept during continued training on the same data; it is not ungrokking in Varma's sense (no shrinking of the training set). It points to the even part of the nonlinearity, not the particular function, as what matters for these tasks, consistent with the activation-swap result of arXiv 2602.16849 and with the exact even part of a SwiGLU unit being bilinear (item 'checked identities'). Single runs: a hypothesis, not a result.

items.question: Q2, Q4, Q6
items.claim: A two-layer ReLU network trained on modular addition keeps perfect accuracy when ReLU is replaced at test time by |x|, x^2, x^4, x^8, log(1+e^(2x)) or e^x, and drops to chance with x or x^3: the learned solution uses only the even-order part of the activation.
items.citation: He, Wang, Chen, Yang (2026), 'On the Mechanism and Dynamics of Modular Addition: Fourier Features, Lottery Ticket, and Grokking', arXiv 2602.16849 v1 (18 Feb 2026).
items.how_read: Sections 2 and 3 (model, empirical findings, Table 1, Observation 4, footnote 2) and the abstract; the remaining 60-page text (proofs, grokking section) not read.
items.finding: Setup: p = 23, width 512, ReLU, AdamW lr 1e-4, trained on the complete dataset without a train/test split for this part. Table 1, accuracy after swapping the activation at test time: max{x,0} 1.000; |x| 1.000; x^2 1.000; x^4 1.000; x^8 1.000; log(1+e^(2x)) 1.000; e^x 1.000; x 0.041; x^3 0.036. Observation 4: 'learning a good solution only relies on the activation's dominant even-order components'. Footnote 2: 'Due to phase symmetry, the output of a ReLU neural network is fundamentally determined by the 1/2 |x| term', from ReLU(x) = (x + |x|)/2. Theory is done with quadratic activation. Abstract: grokking is 'a three-stage process involving memorization followed by two generalization phases, driven by the competition between loss minimization and weight decay'.
items.bears_on: S1, S3, E1, E2, E6. For the Fourier solution of modular addition, ReLU, |x| and x^2 are interchangeable after training: the switching pattern of ReLU is not what carries the computation, its even part is. This makes 'SwiGLU is roughly quadratic' meaningful through the even part, predicts that E1's three nonlinearities can carry the same solution, and is a caution for E2 (a mask transplant tests the ReLU switching pattern, which this result says is replaceable). Accuracy here is on the training data; nothing about generalisation or ungrokking.

items.question: Q1
items.claim: In continual learning, how much an old task is forgotten depends on the activation function, but the ranking of activations changes with the tasks; one proposal designs activations with sparse gradients to reduce forgetting. Varma et al. call ungrokking a special case of catastrophic forgetting, so this is the nearest neighbouring literature.
items.citation: Goodfellow, Mirza, Xiao, Courville, Bengio (2013), 'An Empirical Investigation of Catastrophic Forgetting in Gradient-Based Neural Networks', arXiv 1312.6211 v3. Lan, Mahmood (2023), 'Elephant Neural Networks: Born to Be a Continual Learner', arXiv 2310.01365.
items.how_read: Abstracts only (arXiv listing pages).
items.finding: Goodfellow et al.: two sequential tasks; compared training algorithms and activation functions; 'it is always best to train using the dropout algorithm'; 'different tasks and relationships between tasks result in very different rankings of activation function performance. This suggests the choice of activation function should always be cross-validated.' Lan and Mahmood: 'besides sparse representations, the gradient sparsity of activation functions also plays an important role in reducing forgetting'; replacing classical activations with their 'elephant' activations improves resilience to forgetting.
items.bears_on: S1, E1. Activation functions can modulate forgetting, but in a task-dependent way and with a new task, not by shrinking the training set. No study of ungrokking across activations was found.

items.question: Q1, Q6
items.claim: The reported late collapse of generalisation under continued training on the same data ('anti-grokking') was found in ReLU networks only, without and with weight decay; no activation comparison.
items.citation: Prakash, Martin (2025), 'Grokking and Generalization Collapse: Insights from HTSR theory', arXiv 2506.04434 (4 Jun 2025); Prakash, Martin (2026), 'Late-Stage Generalization Collapse in Grokking: Detecting anti-grokking with Weightwatcher', arXiv 2602.02859.
items.how_read: 2506.04434: abstract. 2602.02859: HTML text copy from the earlier review, searched for activation, ReLU, nonlinearity, weight decay, optimizer, mechanism; passages read.
items.finding: Models: 3-layer ReLU MLP (depth 3, width 200) on a 1k-sample MNIST subset; 1-layer transformer on modular addition with 'ReLU activations, and no LayerNorm'. After about 10^7 steps test accuracy collapses while training accuracy stays perfect; signals are 'Correlation Traps' (outlier singular values of randomised weight matrices) and HTSR alpha < 2, 'in both the cases with (WD>0) and without WD=0 weight decay'; 'activation sparsity, absolute weight entropy, circuit complexity, and l2 weight norms track pre-grokking and grokking but fail to distinguish grokking from anti-grokking' (2506.04434 abstract).
items.bears_on: S1: a loss of generalisation under continued training exists with a fixed activation; no evidence on activations either way.

items.question: Q2
items.claim: Gromov's analytic grokking solution is derived for quadratic activation; the same weights also work with ReLU and GELU, but only at larger width, and trained ReLU networks find the same phase structure. Grokking there needs no regularisation (full-batch GD, MSE).
items.citation: Gromov (2023), 'Grokking modular arithmetic', arXiv 2301.02679 v1. Related theory with quadratic activation: Mohamadi, Li, Wu, Sutherland (2024), 'Why Do You Grok? A Theoretical Analysis of Grokking Modular Addition', arXiv 2407.12332 (ICML 2024).
items.how_read: Gromov: Sections 1 to 3 (setup, analytic solution, generalisations), Appendices B and C, captions of Fig. 3 and Fig. 6. Mohamadi et al.: abstract only.
items.finding: Gromov: two-layer fully connected network, mean-field parametrisation, MSE loss, full-batch GD; 'No explicit regularization is necessary for grokking to occur'; AdamW, weight decay, dropout etc. make grokking happen earlier and at smaller data fractions. With quadratic activation the network 'is cubic in parameters and quadratic in its inputs'; 'The exact results are derived for this particular choice ... while empirical results are only mildly sensitive to the choice of activation function.' 'The weights (6)-(7) also work for other activation functions, including ReLU, however the 100% accuracy is achieved at higher width'; Fig. 6 (test accuracy against width with the analytic weights): 'GELU activation eventually reaches 100% accuracy, but at very large width.' Fig. 3: for networks trained with AdamW or GD, quadratic and ReLU, the phase relation phi1 + phi2 - phi3 is 'strongly peaked around 0'. No grokking-time comparison across activations is reported. Mohamadi et al. (abstract): in the kernel regime no permutation-equivariant model generalises without a constant fraction of the data; 'two-layer quadratic networks that achieve zero training loss with bounded l_infinity norm generalize well with substantially fewer training points'.
items.bears_on: S1, S3, E1. Quadratic activation is the tractable reference model of grokking modular arithmetic, and ReLU nets reach the same Fourier solution. Supports the idea that a degree-2 unit (the bilinear arm of E1) can learn the task; says nothing about ungrokking.

items.question: Q2
items.claim: Grokking, in the sense of test accuracy rising long after training accuracy, occurs in linear networks on linear tasks; it is then an effect of a loss-threshold accuracy metric, not of any nonlinearity. A 2-layer tanh MLP follows the same theory.
items.citation: Levi, Beck, Bar-Sinai (2023), 'Grokking in Linear Estimators - A Solvable Model that Groks without Understanding', arXiv 2310.16441 v1.
items.how_read: Abstract, Sections 1 and 2 (contributions, related work, accuracy definition), Section 4 (two-layer and nonlinear networks, Fig. 5 caption), conclusion.
items.finding: Teacher-student with Gaussian inputs; accuracy = fraction of samples whose loss is below a threshold epsilon. 'Grokking in this setting does not imply any interesting generalization behavior, but rather the simple fact that the generalization loss decays slower than the training loss'; grokking time is mainly set by lambda = d_in / N_tr; L2 regularisation 'suppresses grokking in overparameterized networks'. Section 4.2: 'the dynamics of a 2 layer MLP (1000-200-5) with tanh activations is well approximated by Eqs. (18) and (19)'. 'Some works suggest slingshots or oscillations underlie grokking, but our explanation applies even without these dynamics.'
items.bears_on: S1: delayed generalisation needs no activation function at all. E1's exploratory arm without nonlinearity is therefore not absurd as a grokking model, although Levi's task is linear and the toy's is not.

items.question: Q2
items.claim: Grokking occurs outside neural networks: in Gaussian-process classification and regression, linear regression and Bayesian neural networks.
items.citation: Miller, O'Neill, Bui (2024), 'Grokking Beyond Neural Networks: An Empirical Exploration with Model Complexity', arXiv 2310.17247 v2 (TMLR 03/2024).
items.how_read: Abstract, introduction, Section 2.1 headings and setup passages (zero-one classification with linear regression and with an RBF Gaussian process).
items.finding: 'grokking is not limited to neural networks but occurs in other settings such as Gaussian process (GP) classification, GP regression, linear regression and Bayesian neural networks'; grokking can be induced on algorithmic data 'via the addition of dimensions containing spurious information'; 'grokking may be possible in any model where solution search is guided by complexity and error.' For linear regression 'a very specific set of circumstances were required to induce grokking'.
items.bears_on: S1: the phenomenon class does not depend on an activation function.

items.question: Q2
items.claim: Logistic regression (a linear model) groks when the training data are nearly linearly separable from the origin.
items.citation: Beck, Levi, Bar-Sinai (2025), 'Grokking at the Edge of Linear Separability', arXiv 2410.04489 v2 (ICML 2025 camera-ready).
items.how_read: Abstract only.
items.finding: 'logistic regression can exhibit grokking when the training dataset is nearly linearly separable from the origin and there is strong noise in the perpendicular directions'; near the critical point flat directions with nearly zero gradient make training 'linger for arbitrarily long times near quasi-stable solutions'.
items.bears_on: S1: delayed generalisation with cross-entropy and no hidden nonlinearity.

items.question: Q2, Q5
items.claim: Kernel machines without any learned nonlinearity grok modular arithmetic when their features are learned with the average gradient outer product (Recursive Feature Machines); one-hidden-layer networks with quadratic activation learn the same block-circulant features, and their first-layer weight Gram matrix correlates above 0.92 with the square root of the network's AGOP.
items.citation: Mallinar, Beaglehole, Zhu, Radhakrishnan, Pandit, Belkin (2024), 'Emergence in non-neural models: grokking modular arithmetic via average gradient outer product', arXiv 2407.20199 v3 (9 Jul 2025).
items.how_read: Abstract, Section 2 (AGOP, NFA paragraph), Section 4 (neural networks: NFM, AGOP correlation, random circulant features, AGOP regularisation), Appendix A (NFA statement) and B (training details).
items.finding: Kernel RFM (quadratic or Gaussian Mahalanobis kernel), p = 61: test accuracy jumps after several iterations while training loss is identically zero. NFA as restated: 'for any layer l of a trained neural network with weights W_l, the Neural Feature Matrix (NFM), W_l^T W_l, are highly correlated to the AGOP of the model computed with respect to the input of layer l'; Ansatz 1 (one hidden layer): W1^T W1 proportional to G(f_NN)^alpha, alpha in (0,1], they use alpha = 1/2 'following the main results' of the Science paper. Networks: one hidden layer, quadratic activation, no biases, AdamW, width 1024, batch 32, lr 1e-3, weight decay 1.0, MSE loss. Measured: Pearson correlation of first-layer NFM and sqrt(AGOP) 'greater than 0.92'; random circulant input transforms remove most of the delay at 17.5% training data; AGOP regularisation, like weight decay, gives grokking where no regularisation does not.
items.bears_on: S1 (grokking needs feature learning, not a specific activation), S3 (the neural experiments use a quadratic activation), Q5 (their experiments concern only the first layer).

items.question: Q2, Q6
items.claim: The one controlled comparison of activation functions for grokking time found: in depth-4 MLPs on modular arithmetic, GELU grokked 4.3x faster than ReLU in one hyperparameter regime and not at all in another; the effect interacts with weight decay.
items.citation: Manir, Rupa (2026), 'A Systematic Empirical Study of Grokking: Depth, Architecture, Activation, and Regularization', arXiv 2603.25009 v1 (26 Mar 2026; no journal reference listed).
items.how_read: Full text (PDF converted to text); Sections 1, 4.4, 5.2 to 5.5, Tables 4 and 10, discussion.
items.finding: Measured: Delta T = T_test - T_train (steps), modular addition mod 97, depth-4 MLPs, SGD, 5 seeds, 400,000 steps. Table 4, Sweep A (lr 1e-2, weight decay 2e-3, width 256): GELU 0/5 grokked; ReLU 2/5, mean 266,000 (std 96,167); Tanh 3/5, 242,667 (134,288). Sweep B (lr 3e-2, weight decay 5e-4, width 512): GELU 5/5, 45,600 (5,550); ReLU 5/5, 196,800 (89,728); Tanh 2/5, 188,000 (36,770). Table 10 (multiplication, weight decay 1e-3): GELU 5/5, 24,400; ReLU 5/5, 93,200; Tanh 3/5, 102,667. Authors: 'GELU's advantage only emerges when regularization is light enough to permit memorization'. Transformers (AdamW, weight decay 1.0) were not compared across activations; one transformer seed's longer delay is called 'consistent with the slingshot dynamics'. Caution: the abstract says depth-4 MLPs fail 'consistently', which is true only for one configuration (H1, 0/5), while Sweep B depth-4 MLPs grokked 5/5.
items.bears_on: S1, E1. The activation changes grokking time, but the sign of the effect depends on the weight-decay regime, so E1 run at one setting (AdamW 1e-3, weight decay 0.3) cannot generalise to 'the activation decides'. No ungrokking measured.

items.question: Q2, Q3
items.claim: Without regularisation, grokking tasks drive the logits so large that float32 rounding in the softmax ('Softmax Collapse') zeroes the gradients of correctly classified samples and stops learning; the cause is the 'naive loss minimisation' direction (scaling the weights). Remedies: StableMax (a replacement for softmax), the orthogonal gradient (perpGrad), and weight decay.
items.citation: Prieto, Barsbey, Mediano, Birdal (2025), 'Grokking at the Edge of Numerical Stability', arXiv 2501.04697 v2 (ICLR 2025).
items.how_read: Abstract, Sections 1 to 3, 5.2, 6 (related work), 7, Appendices B.2, C, H and I (PDF converted to text). Section 4 not read.
items.finding: Models: 2-hidden-layer MLP (width 200) and a 1-layer transformer, ReLU, full batch, AdamW or SGD, weight decay 0 unless stated. Fig. 2: as the training fraction falls, generalisation stops when Softmax Collapse begins, 'earlier for float32 than float64'. Weight decay: 'the main roles of weight decay are preventing floating point errors and preventing NLM'. StableMax is called 'a new activation function', but it replaces the output softmax, not the hidden nonlinearity. App. H: 'slingshots could lead to generalization because they prevent full SC ... Whether and how slingshots are caused by SC remains an open research question'. App. I: 'grokking could be stopped before SC due to the eps parameter in Adam being too large ... the second order moments can be dominated by the eps term, putting an end to learning'. App. H also says Nanda et al. 'show that slingshots can disappear when using float64'; in the version of Nanda et al. I read, the statement is the converse (they induced slingshots by lowering precision; see Nanda item).
items.bears_on: S1 (the 'activation function' that matters here is the output softmax and its numerics, not the hidden nonlinearity), E3 (precision of the loss is a candidate cause of the collapses; a larger eps can stop learning altogether).

items.question: Q3
items.claim: The 'slingshot mechanism': late in training, Adam-type optimisers alternate between rapid growth of the last-layer weight norm and a plateau with a training-loss spike. It was found in the toy's exact setup without weight decay, is removed by a larger Adam eps (which also removed generalisation), and persisted as 'instability' with weight decay 0.1 to 1.0. It also occurs in a deep linear network.
items.citation: Thilak, Littwin, Zhai, Saremi, Paiss, Susskind (2022), 'The Slingshot Mechanism: An Empirical Study of Adaptive Optimizers and the Grokking Phenomenon', arXiv 2206.04817 v2.
items.how_read: Sections 1 to 4 in full; Appendices A.0.4 and A.0.5 (deep linear models, optimisers), B (setup), the beta and eps passages of Appendix A, C.1 (weight decay) and C.2 (normalisation). Figures not inspected beyond captions.
items.finding: Setup (Sec. 3.1): decoder-only transformer, 2 layers, width 128, 4 heads, about 450K parameters, division mod p (p = 97 in App. B), Adam lr 1e-3, weight decay 0, betas 0.9/0.98, eps 1e-8, 10 warmup steps, minibatch 512. Slingshots seen with Adam, AdamW, RMSProp; not with Adagrad, SGD, SGD with momentum; also in a 6-layer linear model on 200 CIFAR-10 samples (full-batch AdamW). Cause (hypothesis, Sec. 3.2): for the update x - mu g/(|g| + eps) on a quadratic, 'the condition ||A||_s < 2 eps / mu ... implies that the mapping M_t is a contraction'; 'the smaller eps, the more restrictive the requirements on the top eigenvalue'; 'increasing the value of eps would lift the restriction on the curvature, and with it evidence of Slingshot Effects'. Measured (Fig. 4, division): more slingshot cycles at smaller eps; with eps = 1e-5 no slingshot and 'no sign of generalization even after receiving 500K updates'; Fig. 5: across datasets slingshots 'disappear with higher values of eps'. Weight decay: Sec. 3.3 says with weight decay 'the model does not become unstable', but App. C.1 (weight decay 0 to 1.0, AdamW) says slingshots and grokking delay disappear while 'the model experiences instability ... this regularization does not decrease training instability'. Feature-and-weight normalisation with temperature 0.25 gave stable training in some tasks. The authors 'lack a satisfactory theoretical explanation'.
items.bears_on: Premise 3 and E3. The toy's collapses (norm jumps, brief loss of kept problems, recovery) resemble this documented phenomenon in an almost identical setup, and Thilak's own appendix reports instabilities persisting with weight decay. From their condition, the allowed curvature scales with eps/mu: eps 1e-8 to 1e-5 relaxes it 1000-fold, lr 1e-3 to 3e-4 only 3.3-fold (my arithmetic on their formula). The eps change also removed generalisation from scratch, so in E3 a 5% run that stays generalised under eps = 1e-5 may reflect slowed learning rather than the absence of collapses. Slingshots in a linear network speak against S1 if the collapses are slingshots.

items.question: Q3
items.claim: Nanda et al. saw significant slingshots in 2-layer transformers trained with AdamW and weight decay, could induce them in 1-layer models by lowering the precision of the loss, and found slingshots unnecessary for grokking.
items.citation: Nanda, Chan, Lieberum, Smith, Steinhardt (2023), 'Progress measures for grokking via mechanistic interpretability', arXiv 2301.05217.
items.how_read: Appendix C.2.2 ('2-Layer Transformers') and D.2, plus the training-setup paragraph; HTML text copy from the earlier review, searched for slingshot, float, precision, epsilon.
items.finding: Training: full-batch AdamW, lr 1e-3, weight decay 1. App. D.2: 'our 2-layer transformers exhibit significant slingshots (Thilak et al., 2022) during training. We speculate that this is due to how gradients of different scale interact with adaptive optimizers. We were even able to induce slingshots on a 1-layer by reducing the precision of the loss calculations (as this causes many gradients to round to 0 and thus greatly increases the differences in scale of gradients). However, as many of our 1-layer models do not exhibit slingshots but nonetheless grok, the slingshot mechanism is unnecessary for grokking to occur, in the presence of weight decay or other regularization.' No mention of eps found.
items.bears_on: Premise 3, E3: slingshots occur in 2-layer transformers despite weight decay 1.0, as in the toy (2 blocks, weight decay 0.3). Lower loss precision makes them more likely, which points to a float64-loss control.

items.question: Q3, Q6
items.claim: A NeurIPS 2026 paper argues that slingshot spikes are a floating-point artefact: once the correct-class logit gap exceeds the float32 absorption threshold (about 16), the correct-class gradient rounds to zero, the zero-sum constraint across classes breaks, classifier mean and feature mean grow exponentially ('Numerical Feature Inflation'), and when gradients re-emerge Adam's huge effective step causes the spike. Casting only the logits/loss to float64 removed the spikes.
items.citation: Liu, Cao, Li, Zhou (2026), 'Grokking or Glitching? How Low-Precision Drives Slingshot Loss Spikes', arXiv 2605.06152 v5 (5 Nov 2026; accepted to NeurIPS 2026).
items.how_read: Abstract, Sections 1, 2, 3 (start), 4.1 (start), 4.2 (mitigation study), Appendix A.3 (why slingshots are rare), A.4 (start), Appendix D (hyperparameters).
items.finding: Setup for modular arithmetic (Table 2): p = 97, 2-layer decoder-only transformer (and a 6-layer MLP), Adam lr 1e-3, 10 warmup steps, betas 0.9/0.999, eps 1e-8, weight decay 0, batch 512, 100,000 steps, float32, one seed (42); mitigation runs full batch. Fig. 1a: 'Slingshot loss spikes disappear when training is performed in float64. Casting only the logits/loss computation to float64 is also sufficient to remove the spikes'. Spike step: Adam update jumps from about 1e-5 to about plus or minus 4e-4 (computed and observed). Fig. 3a: 'eps = 1e-6 reduces the frequency of spikes, setting eps = 1e-5 completely eliminates them'; this 'works by lowering the upper bound of the effective learning rate (eta/eps)'. Plain GD with lr 1e5 after the loss reached zero (emulating eta/eps) spiked at about the same epoch but did not recover. Layer norm on the features before the classifier 'fails to mitigate the effect' and 'accelerates the onset'; batch norm right before the classifier eliminates it; label smoothing removes these spikes but brings edge-of-stability spikes. Weight decay and z-loss not tested, 'their ability to mitigate Slingshot has been demonstrated in existing works'; App. A.3.1: AdamW bounds ||w||_inf by about 1/lambda, so the logit margin 'rarely exceeds' about 16. 'Slingshots are most prominent when the batch size is large enough (approximating full-batch dynamics)'; minibatches make simultaneous collapse unlikely 'except in highly structured and nearly noiseless tasks such as modular arithmetic'.
items.bears_on: Premise 3 and E3. Strongest candidate explanation for the toy's collapses, but tested without weight decay. In the toy (read-only check of analysis/ju_space/kv_grok.py): the loss is two float32 cross-entropies, at '=' (answer z) and at z (target always EOS), and the 5% continuation (233 problems, chunks of 512) is full batch. My inference, to be tested: the constant EOS target is the easiest term to drive into softmax collapse. Cheaper and cleaner E3 controls than eps or lr: (a) log, per evaluation, the share of per-example float32 losses that are exactly 0 (or logit gap > 16) for both terms; (b) an arm with logits cast to float64 before the cross-entropy, which leaves the optimiser untouched.

items.question: Q3, Q6
items.claim: Adam loss spikes arise when the second-moment estimate v_t decouples from the current squared gradient and decays on its own, pushing the preconditioned curvature above 2/eta. A smaller learning rate shifts the spike (it occurs when sqrt(v_t) has decayed proportionally further) rather than preventing it; larger eps, v_t clipping or smaller beta2 suppress it.
items.citation: Bai, Zhou, Zhao, Li, Li, Xiong, Yang, Zhang, Xu (2026), 'Adaptive Preconditioners Trigger Loss Spikes in Adam', arXiv 2506.04805 v2 (accepted to ICML 2026).
items.how_read: Abstract, Sections 1 and 3 (quadratic example, Fig. 2 caption), passages of Section 4 (decoupling, mitigation by eps), appendix paragraph 'Controlling Adaptive Preconditioners to Eliminate Spikes'.
items.finding: On f = theta^2/2, 'Adam with a learning rate eta << 2 (beta1 0.9, beta2 0.99, eps 1e-8) still fails to converge'; 'smaller learning rates correspond to smaller sqrt(v_t) values when spikes occur', slope near 1 in log-log; 'Under different learning rates, the ratio eta/sqrt(v_t) consistently reaches a nearly identical threshold value immediately before the loss begins to spike'. 'directly reducing beta2 effectively mitigates loss spikes'. Appendix: 'using a larger eps significantly reduces spike severity by effectively imposing an upper bound on the preconditioned eigenvalues ... increasing eps or applying v_t clipping from the beginning of training can also mitigate spike behavior, although this may come at the cost of slower convergence'.
items.bears_on: E3: by this account a lr reduction from 1e-3 to 3e-4 is expected to delay or thin out spikes, not remove them; eps = 1e-5 is expected to suppress them at the cost of slower learning. The toy's beta2 = 0.98 is already lower than the defaults studied.

items.question: Q3
items.claim: With full-batch Adam the preconditioned sharpness rises to and hovers at the stability threshold 38/eta (beta1 = 0.9); crossing it causes explosive oscillation, large gradients then raise the preconditioner and the cycle repeats. Only at extremely small learning rates did the sharpness stay below the threshold.
items.citation: Cohen, Ghorbani, Krishnan, Agarwal, Medapati, Badura, Suo, Cardoze, Nado, Dahl, Gilmer (2022), 'Adaptive Gradient Methods at the Edge of Stability', arXiv 2207.14484 v2.
items.how_read: Abstract, Sections 1, 2 (preconditioner definition with eps), passages of 3 and 4 (Fig. 9 zoom, role of hyperparameters, corner case), Appendix D (corner case) and the rmsprop self-stabilisation appendix.
items.finding: Preconditioner P = diag(sqrt(nu)) + eps I; threshold on lambda_1(P^-1 H) is 38/eta for Adam with beta1 0.9. Cycle at lr 5e-5: preconditioned sharpness crosses the threshold, 'Adam ... oscillate[s] explosively', 'large gradients ... increase the second-moment accumulator', sharpness drops, 'The cycle then repeats'; at 2e-4 to 4e-4 the instability is resolved catapult-like with both sharpnesses dropping. Small eta or small beta2 lead to sharper solutions. Corner case: 'at extremely small learning rates' (CNN on CIFAR-10, lr 1e-6 to 3.3e-6) the preconditioned sharpness 'fails to rise to the stability threshold'. They say this 'explains' the 'small bumps and large spikes' others saw in full-batch Adam.
items.bears_on: E3: under this picture a smaller learning rate raises the threshold but curvature keeps rising to it, so spikes are expected to move, not vanish, unless lr is extremely small. My derivation from their P: when sqrt(nu) << eps the condition becomes roughly lambda_max(H) < 38 eps/eta, the same eps/eta scaling as in Thilak's toy analysis.

items.question: Q3
items.claim: In large language models (7B to 546B parameters), loss spikes are explained by gradients of some layers falling below eps, becoming time-correlated and then re-emerging, which gives large, sign-like updates. Suggested remedies: lower learning rate, smaller (not larger) eps, smaller batch, resetting the optimiser state.
items.citation: Molybog et al. (Meta AI) (2023), 'A Theory on Adam Instability in Large-Scale Machine Learning', arXiv 2304.09871 v2.
items.how_read: Abstract, introduction, Section 6 (theory as a multi-stage process), Section 7.1 (mitigation).
items.finding: Stages: gradients of a parameter group 'vanishing (<< eps)', updates spike at 0, gradients become time-correlated, the update ratio m/sqrt(v) becomes bimodal, a rare batch lifts gradients above eps and a 'chain reaction' follows; 'the frequency of the spikes increases later in training when the order of magnitude of the gradient estimation entries for the majority of layers drops below eps'. Section 7.1: 'lowering the learning rate, which helps both theoretically and in practice but extends the overall training time. Tuning down the eps value should be considered'; also smaller batch, smaller averaging constants, resetting the optimiser state when a dip statistic signals bimodality. Caveat from the paper: spikes reproduced at smaller scale are 'not necessarily caused by or remediated by the same factors'. They used ReLU instead of SwiGLU.
items.bears_on: E3: at large scale the recommended direction for eps is the opposite of Thilak's; the mechanism differs (gradients below eps). The literature therefore does not support 'larger eps is safe' in general; for the toy, the precision mechanism of arXiv 2605.06152 is closer in setting.

items.question: Q3
items.claim: In CLIP training, loss spikes follow 1 to 8 iterations after AdamW's second-moment estimate under-estimates the squared gradients; spikes grow with model size, batch size and learning rate and are removed by lowering beta2 or by update clipping (StableAdamW). In small language-model proxies, gradient RMS near eps shrinks updates; eps 1e-6 diverged and 1e-15 helped.
items.citation: Wortsman, Dettmers, Zettlemoyer, Morcos, Farhadi, Schmidt (2023), 'Stable and low-precision training for large-scale vision-language models', arXiv 2304.13013 v2. Wortsman, Liu, Xiao, Everett, Alemi et al. (2023), 'Small-scale proxies for large-scale Transformer training instabilities', arXiv 2309.14322 v2.
items.how_read: 2304.13013: abstract, Sections 3.3 and 3.4 (passages; two-column extraction partly garbled). 2309.14322: abstract, Section 3.4 (eps), Section 3.6 (edge of stability and fast spikes), Fig. 11 to 13 captions.
items.finding: 2304.13013: spikes 'consistently occur 1-8 iterations after the squared gradients become under-estimated by their AdamW second moment estimator'; Section 3.3: loss spikes increase with model size, batch size and learning rate (their Figs. 6, 7, 3), they 'can be avoided by reducing the beta2 hyperparameter', but 'if beta2 is reduced too much then learning is slowed'. 2309.14322: 'If the gradient RMS becomes too small without adjusting eps or weight decay, a layer may collapse'; for a 4.8B model at lr 0.3, 'Decreasing eps to 1e-15 improves loss and mitigates a collapse in grad RMS ... increasing eps to 1e-6 results in an instability'. Their reading of Cohen et al.: 'when beta2 is large, H tends to shrink and fast loss spikes result ... when beta2 is small, P^-1 tends to shrink, no loss spikes are observed' (not verified verbatim in Cohen et al.).
items.bears_on: E3: a smaller learning rate reduces spikes in these large-scale settings; eps effects depend on how gradients compare with eps, and can go either way. These are not grokking settings.

items.question: Q3
items.claim: Clipping the gradient norm in grokking runs slowed generalisation but did not prevent it.
items.citation: Notsawo, Zhou, Pezeshki, Rish, Dumas (2023), 'Predicting Grokking Long Before it Happens: A look into the loss landscape of models which grok', arXiv 2306.13253 v3.
items.how_read: Abstract (partial) and the gradient-clipping passage only.
items.finding: 'To reduce this phenomenon (i.e. the amplitude of the spikes), we clipped the gradient norm during training (using a threshold eta > 0). This had the effect of slowing down generalization, but not preventing it.' The paper reads early oscillations of the training loss as a predictor of grokking.
items.bears_on: E3: another intervention on the spikes that changes the speed of the dynamics, the same confound as a larger eps.

items.question: Q4
items.claim: Dauphin et al. compared gated linear units (sigmoid gate), bilinear layers (no gate nonlinearity) and purely linear layers: bilinear was much better than linear and somewhat worse than GLU.
items.citation: Dauphin, Fan, Auli, Grangier (2016/2017), 'Language Modeling with Gated Convolutional Networks', arXiv 1612.08083.
items.how_read: Section 5.3 ('Non-linear Modeling') and the Figure 5 caption.
items.finding: 'Another variation of GLUs are bilinear layers (Mnih & Hinton, 2007) which take the form h_l(X) = (X*W + b) (x) (X*V + c)'. Google Billion Word: 'GLUs perform best, followed by bilinear layers and then linear layers. Bilinear layers improve over linear ones by more than 40 perplexity points, and the GLU improves another 20 perplexity points over the bilinear model. The linear model performs very poorly at perplexity 115 ... the introduction of the bilinear units is enough to reach 61 perplexity'.
items.bears_on: S3, E1, E6: a pure degree-2 gated unit is a strong but not equal substitute for a gated unit with a nonlinear gate (here sigmoid, not SiLU).

items.question: Q4
items.claim: In T5 pre-training the bilinear feed-forward layer is close to SwiGLU and better than ReLU or GELU at matched parameters and compute.
items.citation: Shazeer (2020), 'GLU Variants Improve Transformer', arXiv 2002.05202 v1.
items.how_read: Full text.
items.finding: Definitions: FFN_Bilinear(x) = (xW (x) xV)W2; FFN_SwiGLU(x) = (Swish_1(xW) (x) xV)W2; d_ff reduced from 3072 to 2048 for the three-matrix variants. Table 1, held-out log-perplexity after 65,536 / 524,288 steps (std over 4 short runs): ReLU 1.997 (0.005) / 1.677; GELU 1.983 / 1.679; Swish 1.994 / 1.683; GLU 1.982 / 1.663; Bilinear 1.960 (0.005) / 1.648; GEGLU 1.942 / 1.633; SwiGLU 1.944 (0.010) / 1.636; ReGLU 1.953 / 1.645. The paper offers 'no explanation as to why these architectures seem to work'.
items.bears_on: S3, E1: as a trained architecture, a degree-2 unit gets within about 0.012 nats of SwiGLU. This is a statement about training from scratch, not about how well a bilinear map approximates a given SwiGLU layer.

items.question: Q4
items.claim: Pearce et al. use bilinear MLPs in place of SwiGLU and analyse them through eigendecompositions of interaction matrices. Trained from scratch the loss is slightly worse than SwiGLU at equal data and equal at equal time; a pretrained SwiGLU model (TinyLlama-1.1B) was converted to bilinear by fine-tuning, at about +0.05 loss.
items.citation: Pearce, Dooms, Rigg, Oramas, Sharkey (2025), 'Bilinear MLPs enable weight-based mechanistic interpretability', arXiv 2410.08417 v2 (ICLR 2025).
items.how_read: Abstract, Sections 2 and 3 (bilinear tensor, symmetry, eigendecomposition), 5.2 (low-rank approximations), summary, Appendices G.2, I and J. Text searched for single-neuron or rank-2 statements.
items.finding: Replacement: their language model is 'a 6-layer modern transformer model ... where the SwiGLU is replaced with a bilinear MLP' (about 33M parameters, TinyStories). App. I (6 layers, d_model 512, d_hidden 2048): loss at constant epochs Bilinear 1.337, ReGLU 1.332, SwiGLU 1.321; at constant time 1.337, 1.337, 1.336 ('Bilinear layers are 6% less data efficient but equally compute efficient'). App. J: Swish_beta with beta -> 0 is linear, so they interpolate beta from 1 to 0 over 120M tokens and fine-tune 280M more; 'this fine-tuning process increases the loss by about (0.05)' against a continued-training baseline, gap shrinking with training. Eigenvectors: for an output direction u the interaction matrix Q = u . B is symmetric; 'x^T Q x = sum_i lambda_i (v_i^T x)^2 ... the bilinear layer's outputs are quadratic in the eigenvector basis'; 'The top eigenvectors by eigenvalue magnitude give the best low-rank approximation'. Sec. 5.2: for SAE output features of bilinear transformers, active-only correlation of the low-rank approximation 'starting around 0.65' with one eigenvector; 'Most features have a high correlation (> 0.75) even when approximated by just two eigenvectors'. I found no statement about the two eigenvectors of a single neuron.
items.bears_on: S3, E6, E1: closest published evidence that SwiGLU can be traded for a degree-2 unit at small cost in loss; the conversion needed 400M tokens of fine-tuning, so it is not a measurement of how much of a SwiGLU layer's output is already degree 2.

items.question: Q4
items.claim: Closed-form least-squares polynomial approximations of MLPs and GLUs under Gaussian inputs: for a one-hidden-layer ReLU MLP on MNIST-like inputs the quadratic approximant explains over 95% of the output variance throughout training. GLUs are covered by the derivation, but no SwiGLU measurement is reported.
items.citation: Belrose, Rigg (2025), 'Converting MLPs into Polynomials in Closed Form', arXiv 2502.01032 v1 (3 Feb 2025).
items.how_read: Abstract, introduction, Section 3.5 (start), Sections 4.1 and 4.2, conclusion passage; text searched for GLU, SwiGLU, transformer.
items.finding: Experiment: single hidden layer ReLU MLP on MNIST, schedule-free AdamW, weight decay 0.1, batch 64; approximants fitted under Gaussian-mixture inputs matched to the MNIST class means and covariances; measured fraction of variance unexplained (FVU) across checkpoints. Linear FVU rises sharply between 500 and 1K steps ('quadratic phase'), quadratic FVU stays nearly constant; 'quadratics explaining well over 95% of the variance in MLP outputs'. The bilinear layer 'has similar performance to GLUs with nonlinearities like Swish (SwiGLU) or ReLU (ReGLU)' (citing Shazeer).
items.bears_on: S3, E6: the nearest measured statement, but for a ReLU MLP on near-Gaussian image inputs, not for a trained SwiGLU layer on its real inputs. E6 (b) and (c) would be new measurements as far as I found.

items.question: Q4
items.claim: Quadratic neurons and polynomial networks are an established line: products of linear maps give networks whose output is a polynomial of the input, which can work even without activation functions.
items.citation: Fan, Xiong, Wang (2018/2019), 'Universal Approximation with Quadratic Deep Networks', arXiv 1808.00098 v3. Chrysos, Moschoglou, Bouritsas, Panagakis, Deng, Zafeiriou (2020), 'Pi-nets: Deep Polynomial Neural Networks', arXiv 2003.03828 (CVPR 2020). Kileel, Trager, Bruna (2019), 'On the Expressive Power of Deep Polynomial Neural Networks', arXiv 1905.12207. Sharkey (2023), 'A technical note on bilinear layers for interpretability', arXiv 2305.03452.
items.how_read: Abstracts only.
items.finding: Fan et al.: a quadratic neuron replaces the inner product with a quadratic function; four theorems on expressive efficiency against conventional networks. Chrysos et al.: Pi-nets, 'the output is a high-order polynomial of the input', implemented with special skip connections, parameters as high-order tensors; 'they even produce good results without the use of non-linear activation functions'. Kileel et al.: networks with polynomial activations define an algebraic map from weights to polynomials; the dimension of its image variety as a measure of expressivity. Sharkey: bilinear layers 'can be expressed using only linear operations and third order tensors', 'performing better than standard MLPs' (claim from the abstract).
items.bears_on: S3, S4, E9 point 5: stacking bilinear (degree-2) layers multiplies degrees, which is the polynomial-network view the plan uses for representing a cubic with two layers.

items.question: Q4, Q5
items.claim: Checked mathematics (not a literature result): for SiLU, GELU and ReLU, phi(g) - phi(-g) = g. Hence the part of a gated unit phi(g) u (g, u linear in the input) that is even under input sign flip is exactly g u / 2, a polynomial of degree at most 2; for SwiGLU the rest is (g/2) tanh(g/2) u. A single bilinear neuron's symmetric interaction matrix has its two eigenvectors along the bisectors of its weight vectors.
items.citation: Own derivation, checked numerically (python, double precision) in this review.
items.how_read: Not applicable (computation): sympy series of x/(1+e^-x); maximum deviations on a grid g in [-12, 12]; eigendecomposition of (w v^T + v w^T)/2 for random w, v.
items.finding: silu(g) = g/2 + (g/2) tanh(g/2) (max deviation 3.6e-15); silu(g) - silu(-g) = g (1.8e-15); same identity for GELU (8.9e-16) and ReLU (0); even part of silu(w.x)(v.x) under x -> -x equals (w.x)(v.x)/2 (8.9e-16). Series: silu(g) = g/2 + g^2/4 - g^4/48 + g^6/480 + O(g^8), so near g = 0 a SwiGLU unit is g u/2 + g^2 u/4 + ...; for large positive g it tends to g u, for large negative g to 0. Single neuron: nonzero eigenvalues |w||v|(cos phi + 1)/2 and |w||v|(cos phi - 1)/2 with eigenvectors w/|w| + v/|v| and w/|w| - v/|v| (matches the plan's E6 statement); equivalently (a.x)(b.x) = [((a+b).x)^2 - ((a-b).x)^2]/4 for unit a, b, the polarisation identity of the multiplication gate.
items.bears_on: S3, E6: 'SwiGLU is roughly quadratic' has an exact version: its input-even half is exactly bilinear; the other half is odd in the input and is degree 3 near the origin and like |g| u/2 far from it. A variance split into the even part g u/2 and the odd rest is distribution-free and could stand next to E6's least-squares line split. Together with arXiv 2602.16849 (solutions use the even part of the activation) this suggests measuring which half carries the toy's computation.

items.question: Q5
items.claim: Lin, Tegmark and Rolnick build a multiplication gate from four neurons of any smooth activation with a nonzero second derivative; it is the polarisation identity uv = ((u+v)^2 - (u-v)^2)/4 realised through the even part of the activation.
items.citation: Lin, Tegmark, Rolnick (2017), 'Why does deep and cheap learning work so well?', arXiv 1608.08225 v4 (3 Aug 2017).
items.how_read: Section on continuous input variables: theorem, equation (11), Fig. 2 and footnote 3.
items.finding: Network f = A2 sigma A1 with layer sizes 2, 4, 1. Eq. (10): sigma(u) = sigma0 + sigma1 u + sigma2 u^2/2 + O(u^3); eq. (11): m(u, v) = [sigma(u+v) + sigma(-u-v) - sigma(u-v) - sigma(-u+v)] / (4 sigma2) = uv [1 + O(u^2 + v^2)], so sigma2 = sigma''(0) (Fig. 2 labels it 4 sigma''(0)); 'since sigma is non-linear, it must have a non-zero second derivative at some point, so we can use the biases in A1 to shift the origin to this point'; scaling A1 -> lambda A1, A2 -> lambda^-2 A2 makes it exact as lambda -> infinity: 'arbitrarily accurate multiplication can always be achieved using merely 4 neurons'; 'a reasonably good approximation can be achieved already for lambda^-1 ~ 10'. Corollary: a polynomial needs about 4 neurons per multiplication. The construction is stated for 'any smooth but otherwise arbitrary non-linearity'; ReLU is mentioned only as generating piecewise linear functions.
items.bears_on: S3, E6, E7: the network-level counterpart of the bisector picture (u+v and u-v). With a quadratic or bilinear unit the gate is exact with 2 squares or 1 unit.

items.question: Q5
items.claim: Yarotsky builds multiplication in deep ReLU networks from squaring, using xy = ((x+y)^2 - x^2 - y^2)/2 (not the (x+y)^2 - (x-y)^2 form), with x^2 approximated by sawtooth functions to error eps at depth and size O(ln(1/eps)).
items.citation: Yarotsky (2017), 'Error bounds for approximations with deep ReLU networks', arXiv 1610.01145 v3.
items.how_read: Section 3.1 (Propositions 2 and 3, equation (3)).
items.finding: Proposition 2: 'The function f(x) = x^2 on the segment [0, 1] can be approximated with any error eps > 0 by a ReLU network having the depth and the number of weights and computation units O(ln(1/eps))', via f_{m-1}(x) - f_m(x) = g_m(x)/2^(2m) with the iterated tooth function g. Equation (3): 'xy = 1/2 ((x + y)^2 - x^2 - y^2)'. Proposition 3: for |x|, |y| <= M a ReLU network gives |x~y - xy| <= eps with the same logarithmic complexity.
items.bears_on: S3, E9 point 5: with ReLU, products and polynomials need depth; a quadratic or bilinear unit has them built in.

items.question: Q5
items.claim: The (Deep) Neural Feature Ansatz is stated for every layer, but it relates a layer's weight Gram matrix to the average gradient outer product of the TRAINED network taken with respect to THAT LAYER'S INPUT. Only for the first layer (scalar output) is it an expected gradient outer product in input space. The project's finding (last hidden layer varies along the top eigenvector of the target's gradient outer product in input coordinates) is therefore not an instance of it.
items.citation: Radhakrishnan, Beaglehole, Pandit, Belkin, arXiv 2212.13881 v3 (9 May 2023), titled 'Mechanism of feature learning in deep fully connected networks and kernel machines that recursively learn features'; published as 'Mechanism for feature learning in neural networks and backpropagation-free machine learning models', Science 383, 1461-1467 (2024).
items.how_read: arXiv v3: abstract, Section 2 (statement of the ansatz, Fig. 2 and caption, validation across nonlinearities). The Science version was not read.
items.finding: Exact statement: 'we posit that the NFM of any layer of a trained network is proportional to the average gradient outer product of the network taken with respect to the input to this layer. In particular, let W_i denote the weights of layer i ..., let h_i(x) denote the input into layer i of the network, and let f_i denote the sub-network of f operating on h_i(x) ... W_i^T W_i proportional to sum_p grad f_i(h_i(x_p)) grad f_i(h_i(x_p))^T'. 'We note that for the special case of the first layer and for networks with scalar outputs, the right hand side is related to the statistical estimator known as the expected gradient outer product'. Measured: 5-hidden-layer ReLU networks, 1024 units, 121 tabular tasks: median Pearson correlation of trained NFM and AGOP above 0.85 per layer; CelebA: layers 2-5 > 0.78, layer 1 0.99; also for leaky ReLU, tanh, sigmoid, sine and Adam. Mallinar et al. (arXiv 2407.20199) restate it as W1^T W1 proportional to AGOP^alpha with alpha = 1/2, citing the Science version; their experiments use only the first layer.
items.bears_on: S3, E7. (1) The ansatz is about weights, not about the input directions along which a layer's activations vary; (2) for deeper layers the gradient is with respect to that layer's input, not the network input; (3) it concerns the trained network's AGOP, which equals the target's only as far as the network fits. The project's result connects to it only through the first layer: if W1^T W1 aligns with (a power of) the input-space AGOP and the fit is good, every later layer, being a function of W1 x, sees the input mainly through the dominant directions of the target's gradient outer product. That chain is my inference; no paper states it for the last hidden layer. The plan's reading (8.7: the post's finding 'follows from the task') is compatible with this literature but not a quotation of it.

items.question: Q6, Q2
items.claim: 2026 'delay law' papers model grokking time through the weight norm and the optimiser, not the activation; one finds that a final layer norm removes the norm dependence by decoupling weight scale from the function, another that SGD fails where AdamW groks.
items.citation: Khanh, Hoa, Trung, Duc (2026), 'The Norm-Separation Delay Law of Grokking', arXiv 2603.13331 v2. Khanh, Hoa, Trung, Duc (2026), 'First-Passage Prediction of Grokking Delay', arXiv 2605.18845. Khanh, Viet, Trung, Duc (2026), 'The Weight Norm Sets the Grokking Timescale: A Causal Delay Law', arXiv 2606.13753.
items.how_read: Abstracts only.
items.finding: 2603.13331: T_grok - T_mem = Theta(gamma_eff^-1 log(||theta_mem||^2 / ||theta_post||^2)), gamma_eff = eta lambda for SGD, >= eta lambda for AdamW; 293 runs; 'SGD fails entirely at the same hyperparameters where AdamW reliably groks'. 2605.18845: 'Causal interventions that freeze the norm or remove weight decay at memorisation eliminate grokking (0/6 vs. 3/3 baseline)'. 2606.13753: clamping the norm at rho times the critical norm gives T_grok proportional to exp(alpha rho), alpha about 7.5; 'A final LayerNorm removes the dependence by decoupling weight scale from the network function'.
items.bears_on: S1 (no activation dependence studied), E3: in a network with layer norm after each sub-block, as the toy, jumps of the total weight norm are only partly tied to the function; the E3 event criterion 'weight norm rising by 1 or more' should be reported next to a function-level signal (kept-problem accuracy or loss).

items.question: Q6
items.claim: Other 2025-2026 work on how the activation or multiplicative structure shapes grokking: ReLU MLPs learn square-wave (not sinusoidal) input weights whose algorithm is present before grokking; embeddings plus their 'bilinear coupling' with downstream weights cause the delay in MLPs; ReLU-network linear regions migrate during grokking.
items.citation: Swaroop (2026), 'Latent Algorithmic Structure Precedes Grokking: A Mechanistic Study of ReLU MLPs on Modular Arithmetic', arXiv 2603.23784 v2. AlQuabeh, Bojkovic, Nwadike, Inui et al. (2025), 'Mechanistic Insights into Grokking from the Embedding Layer', arXiv 2505.15624. Humayun, Balestriero, Baraniuk (2024), 'Deep Networks Always Grok and Here is Why', arXiv 2402.15555 (ICML 2024).
items.how_read: Abstracts only.
items.finding: Swaroop: 'ReLU MLPs in our setting instead learn near-binary square-wave input weights' with output phases phi_out about phi_a + phi_b, present 'even in models that do not grok'; idealised weights give 95.8% accuracy from models at 0.40%. AlQuabeh et al.: 'introducing [embeddings] into MLPs induces delayed generalization ... whereas MLPs without embeddings can generalize immediately'; mechanisms: sparse updates of rare tokens under weight decay, and 'Bilinear coupling' between embeddings and downstream weights (a product of parameter matrices, not a bilinear activation). Humayun et al.: local complexity (density of linear regions of the spline partition) as a progress measure; regions migrate away from training points toward the decision boundary.
items.bears_on: S1, E2, E8: the activation shapes the learned features (square waves under ReLU), and a ReLU-specific account (linear regions) exists, which is the natural frame for E2's mask transplant; it does not transfer to bilinear or SwiGLU units. None of these studies ungrokking.

items.question: Q6
items.claim: Search record for Q6 (and gaps of Q1 to Q4).

users_premises.premise: ungrokking is caused by the activation function
users_premises.detail: No paper relates ungrokking to the activation function or compares activations for ungrokking. The paper that defined ungrokking (arXiv 2309.02390) explains it by training-set size below a critical size plus weight decay (circuit efficiency); final ungrokked accuracy does not depend on weight-decay strength; the activation enters only a toy model as a homogeneity exponent and is never varied. Against the strong form 'in the end': delayed generalisation occurs in models with no hidden nonlinearity (arXiv 2310.16441, 2410.04489, 2310.17247, 2407.20199), and slingshot instabilities occur in a 6-layer linear network (arXiv 2206.04817). For it, in a weak form: activation choice changes grokking time in a regime-dependent way (arXiv 2603.25009), an odd x^3 activation lost generalisation after a peak in single runs (arXiv 2411.05353), and modular-addition networks rely on the even part of the activation (arXiv 2602.16849). E1 would be the first direct test.

users_premises.premise: SwiGLU is roughly a quadratic polynomial
users_premises.detail: Exactly true for half of it: since silu(g) = g/2 + (g/2) tanh(g/2), the input-even part of every SwiGLU unit is the bilinear (degree-2) term g u/2; the odd rest is about g^2 u/4 near g = 0 (degree 3) and about |g| u/2 for large |g|, so far from the origin a unit is either about g u (open gate) or about 0 (closed gate): piecewise bilinear rather than one quadratic. As trained architectures, bilinear (pure degree-2) units come within about 0.01 nats of SwiGLU (arXiv 2002.05202: 1.648 vs 1.636; arXiv 2410.08417: 1.337 vs 1.321 at equal data, equal at equal time), and a pretrained SwiGLU model was converted to bilinear by fine-tuning at about +0.05 loss (arXiv 2410.08417, App. J). No paper measures how much of a trained SwiGLU layer's output a degree-2 approximation captures; the >95% of arXiv 2502.01032 is for a ReLU MLP on MNIST-like inputs. Whether the Wolfram-post regularities then 'apply' is not addressed by any of these sources.

users_premises.premise: the collapses of training in the toy are a known phenomenon of the optimiser
users_premises.detail: Periodic late-training spikes with weight-norm growth are documented in nearly the toy's exact setup (2-layer transformer, division mod 97, Adam lr 1e-3, betas 0.9/0.98, eps 1e-8, batch 512; arXiv 2206.04817), persist as instabilities with weight decay 0.1 to 1.0 in that setup (its App. C.1) and occur in 2-layer transformers with AdamW and weight decay 1.0 (arXiv 2301.05217, App. D.2). The cause is contested: an adaptive-optimiser curvature limit set by eps/eta (Thilak), Adam's second moment decoupling from the gradient (arXiv 2506.04805), edge of stability (arXiv 2207.14484), or float32 absorption in the cross-entropy that Adam's maximal step eta/eps turns into a spike (arXiv 2605.06152, which removed the spikes by computing only the loss in float64 and made plain GD with an equally large step spike too). So 'known phenomenon' yes; 'of the optimiser' only partly (the optimiser amplifies, numerics may trigger). That the toy's events are this phenomenon has not been shown: no float64-loss control, softmax-collapse share or last-layer norm has been measured.

literature: self-monitoring, the posts o.summary: Block B (decisive for S3 and E7): the earlier LessWrong-based note is right and README 8.7 is wrong on the network. The post's main network is a ReLU MLP 3-64-64-64-15-1 (text: 'four hidden layers ... linear component followed by a ReLU activation ... 64, 64, 64 and 15'; code NetChain[{64, Ramp, 64, Ramp, 64, Ramp, 15, Ramp, 1}]; 9,567 parameters, which matches 64-64-64-15 exactly). It was trained on 500,000 uniform samples in [-3,3]^3 with batch 512 and at most 300 rounds; the optimiser is not named. The '15x15x15x15' sentence refers only to the 49 single-polynomial networks at the end. The notebook with all code is linked from the post and downloadable, and so are the trained net and the SAE weights. The project's local text copy lacks the whole introduction, which explains the README's error. README 8.7 is correct on the SAE (64 features, top-4, last hidden layer, R^2 0.996 on standardised post-ReLU activations), on the nine c values (0.175 to 0.35, median 0.30) and on the vertical stretch. It overstates 'only on t' (R^2 0.88 to 0.985) and 'independent of b' (two b values, compared by eye). The features were also picked by eye, not 'found by the SAE'. So the post's observation comes from a ReLU network, not a quadratic unit. Block A: no source shows a network representing its own activation function or the state of its own MLP gates. The monitoring work (Ji-An et al.; Lindsey; Binder et al.) concerns residual-stream directions or behaviour; Ji-An et al. say explicitly that MLP activations were not studied. Even this is contested in 2026: Singh, Linzen and Ravfogel show that the Ji-An labels are predictable from layer-0 inputs and that Lindsey-style detection does not separate activation steering from prompt manipulation; Ferrara finds no open-weight model above chance. 'Gate' features in Macar et al. are transcoder features, not GLU gates. The closest analogues are trained attention schemas, where networks predict their own attention scores. Premakumar et al. do not detach the self-model target (both prediction and target depend on the weights). They report lower final-layer weight spread and RLCT with self-modelling. Their only control is a baseline without self-modelling: no activation-regularisation control, no non-self target, and the self-model accuracy is not reported. When asked on LessWrong, the authors called an activation-regularisation comparison 'a great idea' and put it on their roadmap. In their MNIST and IMDB set-ups the identity map solves the auxiliary task exactly. The self-predictive-learning literature (SimSiam, Tang et al., NextLat) uses stop-gradient to prevent collapse. I found no work that links self-modelling or self-modifying weights with grokking. Activation-level regularisers do speed up grokking (UFO, GeomDR, Howe 2026; abstracts only). Block C: Pehlivan and Williams' Theorem 1 is as the plan says: R s^3 + S s^2 + T = 0 with no linear term, for the trisector CQ next to side CA. It follows from the angle-bisector length formula applied to the two overlapping triangles CBQ and CPA plus cos 3θ = 4cos^3 θ − 3cos θ. I checked it symbolically and on 20,000 random triangles; the printed squared equation has a typo (4ab²s² for 4ab²s) that does not affect the result. In w = 1/s the cubic is depressed. In σ = h_c/s it becomes exactly the sine triple-angle equation 4σ^3 − 3σ + sin(3A + C) = 0, with σ = sin(A + C/3) (my own derivation, verified). I found no work on networks that solve cubics by Cardano or Viète or that trisect angles. In the grokking papers, products of trigonometric features implement angle addition (Nanda), Pizza averages the two embeddings and doubles the angle with absolute values (Zhong), and quadratic or x^S activations supply the products (Gromov, Doshi). None of these papers uses the words bisection, trisection, triple angle or Chebyshev.

items.finding: The earlier note is right. Notebook and LessWrong text (same wording): 'We choose a simple multi layer perceptron (MLP) infrastructure that takes a 3-dimensional input vector and passes it through four hidden layers. Each layer has a linear component followed by a ReLU activation. The dimensions of the layers are, respectively, 64, 64, 64 and 15. The final 15-dim vector is passed through a linear layer that outputs a single real number y.' Code: net = NetChain[{64, Ramp, 64, Ramp, 64, Ramp, 15, Ramp, 1}, "Input" -> 3, "Output" -> "Scalar"] (Ramp = max(0, x)). The text gives P = 9567 parameters. That matches 3-64-64-64-15-1 exactly (256 + 4160 + 4160 + 975 + 16, my arithmetic); 3-15-15-15-15-1 would have 796. Training code: SeedRandom[1234]; 500,000 samples (x, a, b), each uniform in [-3, 3], target x^3 + a x^2 + x + b; ValidationSet -> Scaled[0.05]; BatchSize -> 512; MaxTrainingRounds -> 300; checkpoints every 10 rounds. The text and code name neither an optimiser nor a loss, so NetTrain defaults apply. The NetTrain documentation, read via the fetch tool, gives Method -> Automatic and lists ADAM, RMSProp, SGD and SignSGD but does not say which one Automatic picks. It names MeanSquaredLossLayer as the default loss for a non-softmax output. The number of rounds actually run is not stated. Text: 'lossless regression (corresponding to a loss equal to 10^-3 on validation dataset) in less than 15 minutes of training on my M2 Pro CPU'. If all 300 rounds ran, that is about 300 x 928 = 2.8e5 batches (my arithmetic). The analysed net is loaded with CloudImport from https://www.wolframcloud.com/obj/enricobottazzi/net.wxf. The sentence 'I trained an NN of size 15x15x15x15' belongs to the closing 'early result' about 49 networks, each regressing a single polynomial from x alone. Training range of x, a, b: [-3, 3] each (text and code).

items.finding: Supported. Text: 'we train a SAE on top of the last 15-dim activation layer of our NN ... a 64-dim SAE with TopK=4. This means that it would be trained to learn 64 features and each encoded activation will be expressed in, at most, 4 features. To train the SAE, we sample 200k activations ... for random input combinations (x,a,b) ... z = ReLU(Wa+b) ... â = zD ... The R^2 coefficient of the trained SAE is 0.995'. Code details: activations come from NetPort["8"], the output of the fourth Ramp (code comment '15-dim, post-Ramp'). The 200,000 points are uniform in [-3,3]^3 (SeedRandom[7]). Activations of all four hidden layers were exported, but the SAE was trained only on the layer-4 file, with an external Python script. Each unit is standardised as (a − mean)/(std + 1e-5) with stored statistics. The code then encodes with the top 4 of max(0, W a_std + b), decodes with z.D and unstandardises; no decoder bias appears in the Wolfram code. The stored validation R^2 printed in the notebook is 0.9959893. Per-example relative reconstruction errors printed in the notebook are 0.158 at one random point and 0.048 at (x, a, b) = (1, 1, 3).

items.question: B3: Exact procedure of the bucket test.
items.claim: README 8.7 (Gegenprobe): x + c·a in 50 buckets, fitted on 10,000 points, tested on 10,000 others, c in steps of 0.025.
items.citation: Bottazzi 2026, notebook cells 'The next step to better describe these features ...', the c-test cells and function r2ForC in 'Code Library'; LessWrong text has the same six steps.
items.how_read: Full text and code of the notebook.
items.finding: Text steps: '1. Pick a candidate value c; 2. For a set of train combinations (x,a,b), compute t = x + ca; 3. Based on the resulting value t, chop the train combinations into 50 buckets; 4. For each bucket, compute the average activation ...; 5. For each test combination, compute t = x + ca, assign it to a bucket, and read off that bucket's average activation as the guess ...; 6. Compute the R^2 score ...'; 'candidate c values in the range [-1, 1]'. The code is r2ForC with nBins = 50. It draws 20,000 points (x, a, b) uniform in [-3,3]^3 (no seed set in that cell) and splits them at random 50/50 (10,000 train, 10,000 test). The c grid is Range[-1, 1, 0.025] (81 values). The 50 buckets are of equal width between the minimum and maximum of t over the training points; test points outside that range are clipped into the end buckets, and empty buckets get the training mean. R^2 = 1 − SS_res/SS_tot, with SS_tot taken about the training mean; the best c is the argmax. b is drawn at random and not used by the predictor, so 1 − R^2 also contains any dependence on b.
items.bears_on: E7 (the project's cubic_direction.py uses equal-count quantile buckets and SS_tot about the test mean, whereas the notebook uses equal-width buckets over the training range; small, but not the same procedure); README 8.7 Gegenprobe

items.finding: Set-up: 'we augmented the output layer to predict both the class probabilities and the activations of specific target layers within the network'. The loss is L = w_c L_c + (w_s/n)(â − a)^2. Target not detached: 'in this auxiliary loss, both â and a were functions of the model weights. A priori, the optimizer did not prefer adjusting the weights responsible for one or the other.' No normalisation of the target is mentioned. MNIST: MLP with one hidden layer of 64, 128, 256 or 512 units; target is the hidden layer; auxiliary weight AW = 1, 5, 10, 20, 50; 50 epochs; SGD lr 0.005, momentum 0.9, Nesterov, batch 64. CIFAR-10: ResNet-18 plus an added linear hidden layer of width 2000. The target is that hidden layer and its input; AW = 0.5, 1, 2; Adam lr 0.001, batch 64, data augmentation. The text says 150 epochs, while the figures show epochs 1 to 250 with RLCT 'from epoch 250'. IMDB: EmbeddingBag (dim 64) feeding a linear hidden layer (128) and a linear output; target is the hidden layer; AW = 100 or 500; 500 epochs; SGD lr 0.1, batch 64. Each variant has 10 seeds, reported as mean with 95 % CI. In MNIST and IMDB the self-model reads the very layer it predicts, so W = I solves the auxiliary task exactly. The authors write the loss as ||(W − I)a + b||^2 in their LessWrong reply.
items.bears_on: S2; E5 (selfmon corresponds to their full-gradient set-up; E5's batch standardisation of targets and its read-out from a later state differ from theirs)

items.question: A1b: Premakumar et al.: what was measured, how large are the effects, which controls?
items.claim: Self-modelling makes networks 'simpler, more regularized, more parameter-efficient'.
items.citation: Premakumar et al., arXiv 2407.10188v2, Results, Figures 2 to 4, Supplement (RLCT calibration).
items.how_read: Full text. Effect sizes read off the figures by eye; they are approximate, because the paper gives no tables.
items.finding: Measures: the SD of the final-layer weights, after pruning the self-model outputs, and the local learning coefficient (RLCT) of the classification loss, estimated with SGLD. SGLD hyperparameters were chosen by 'a qualitative appraisal of the loss curves', and the authors note relatively low MALA acceptance rates. Accuracy on the primary task is also reported. Approximate effects: MNIST, hidden 512, epoch 50: weight SD ≈ 0.097 (baseline) vs ≈ 0.081 (AW 50); RLCT ≈ 58 vs ≈ 37. With hidden 64 or 128 at AW 20 or 50, the primary task broke down (accuracy ≈ 0.11 to 0.27) and the RLCT came out negative, which the authors call 'anomalous'. CIFAR-10: RLCT ≈ 82 vs ≈ 72, 69.5, 66 (AW 0.5, 1, 2). Accuracy ≈ 0.920 vs 0.918 to 0.920, so no gain. Weight-SD differences are small and not monotone in AW. IMDB: RLCT ≈ 13.6 vs ≈ 11 (AW 100) and ≈ 5 (AW 500); accuracy ≈ 0.819 vs ≈ 0.820 and ≈ 0.836; weight SD at epoch 500 ≈ 2.0 vs ≈ 1.6 and ≈ 0.8. Controls: only a network without self-modelling. There is no activation-regularisation control, no non-self target, no weight-decay arm (none used) and no report of the self-model's own prediction accuracy. A commenter on the authors' LessWrong post argued that self-modelling may act as a disguised activation regulariser. The authors replied: 'Comparing the complexity measures (SD & RLCT) between self-modeling and activation regularization is a great idea and we will definitely add this to the roadmap and report back. And batch norm/other forms of regularization were not added.'
items.bears_on: S2; E5 (add an activation-regularisation arm, e.g. an L2 penalty on the gate factors at matched gradient norm, and report the read-out's accuracy; 'othermon' alone does not separate self-modelling from activation shrinkage)

items.citation: Authors' post 'Self-prediction acts as an emergent regularizer', LessWrong, 23 Oct 2024 (post 5se67gAcaExEYdCCg) and its comments; K. T. Farrell, K. Ziman, M. S. A. (same lab) trained ViT-based agents with an 'attention schema', a learned prediction of their own final attention, with weight 0.05 against 0.95 for the task.
