items.question: A2a: Ji-An et al.: what can models report or control, and what limits do the authors state?
items.claim: S2: a network that monitors its own activations may represent its activation function (SwiGLU).
items.citation: L. Ji-An, H.-D. Xiong, R. C. Wilson, M. G. Mattar, M. K. Benna, 'Language Models Are Capable of Metacognitive Monitoring and Control of Their Internal Activations', arXiv 2505.13763v2 (24 Oct 2025).
items.how_read: Main text sections 1 to 5 and appendix A.1 to A.5, B.3 and B.4 in full (arXiv HTML); figure values not read.
items.finding: Labels: the residual-stream activation at layer l, averaged over the sentence's tokens and projected onto an axis, binarised at the median. The axis is either a logistic-regression axis fitted to dataset labels (e.g. ETHICS morality) or a PCA axis. The model learns the mapping in context, with N up to 256 examples. Reporting: the model predicts the label of a new sentence. Accuracy rises with N and is best for the LR axis and early PCs, but stays 'significantly lower than that of the ideal observer' (a linear classifier on the activations). Control: the model is told to imitate label 0 or 1. In explicit control it generates the sentence; in implicit control the sentence is given. The effect is measured as Cohen's d along the axis. Implicit control is 'much smaller', near zero in early layers, and off-target effects show 'limited' precision. Models: Llama-3.x 1B to 70B and Qwen2.5 1B to 7B; datasets ETHICS, True-False, Emotion, Sycophancy. Stated limits: a low-dimensional 'metacognitive space'; and 'while our analysis focused exclusively on the residual stream, other model components — such as attention head outputs, intermediate MLP activations, and layer-wise logits — warrant investigation.' Nothing concerns MLP neurons, gates or the activation function.

items.question: A2b: Is the Ji-An / Lindsey evidence itself robust? (2026 critique)
items.claim: Monitoring of own activations is established.
items.citation: S. Singh, T. Linzen, S. Ravfogel, 'Can LLMs Introspect? A Reality Check', arXiv 2605.26242v2 (21 Aug 2026).
items.how_read: Sections 3 to 5 and appendix A (limitations) in full; figures not viewed.
items.finding: For the Ji-An paradigm (Llama-3.1-8B and 70B, Qwen-2.5-7B-1M), the authors randomly permuted the labels before training the LR probe. In-context accuracy then 'drops to close to the majority-class baseline'. Probes on layer-0 (input-embedding) representations 'match or exceed the models' own in-context predictions of the PCA-derived labels'. So the original results 'do not demonstrate privileged access to internal representations', and the control results 'are equally consistent with being able to control generation'. For Lindsey-style injection they added a 'gaslight' condition: the prompt tells the model to steer toward a concept, with no change to its activations. In the two-way task (no intervention vs activation intervention), Llama-3.1-70B and Qwen-3-32B reproduce Lindsey's pattern. But they also label gaslight trials as activation interventions. In the three-way task (no intervention, input intervention, activation intervention) they fail to separate the two kinds of intervention. Conclusion: 'current evidence is insufficient to establish metacognitive monitoring in LLMs.'
items.bears_on: S2; E4 (decodability of a quantity from states is not monitoring by the network itself); users_premises 1

items.question: A2c: Binder et al.: what can models report, and what limits do the authors state?
items.claim: Models can learn about themselves by introspection.
items.citation: F. J. Binder et al., 'Looking Inward: Language Models Can Learn About Themselves by Introspection', arXiv 2410.13787v1 (17 Oct 2024).
items.how_read: Abstract, sections 2, 3, 4 and 6 in full; appendix not read.
items.finding: The paper is about behaviour, not activations. Models were fine-tuned on 30,000 examples to predict properties of their own answers in hypothetical situations, such as the second character of the response. Self-prediction beats cross-prediction by another model trained on the same behaviour: Llama-3-70B predicting itself 48.5 % vs GPT-4o predicting it 31.8 %; GPT-4o predicting itself 49.4 % vs Llama predicting it 36.6 %. GPT-3.5 gains only +0.8 %. Cross-prediction plateaus at 35.2 % beyond 10,000 samples. Calibration (MAD) improves from 23.0 to 8.7 after self-training vs 21.3 after cross-training. After its behaviour was changed by further fine-tuning, GPT-4o predicted the new behaviour at 35.4 % vs 21.7 % for the old. Stated limits: introspection only on simple tasks; failure on properties of longer responses (e.g. 'predict the length of your response'); no self-advantage for sycophancy (self 74.5 % vs cross 76.5 %); no generalisation to other self-knowledge datasets.
items.bears_on: S2 (no bearing on activation functions)

items.question: A2d: Lindsey: what can models report or control, and what limits are stated?
items.claim: Models have some introspective awareness of internal states.
items.citation: J. Lindsey, 'Emergent Introspective Awareness in Large Language Models', Transformer Circuits Thread, Anthropic, published 29 Oct 2025, revised 1 Jan 2026, https://transformer-circuits.pub/2025/introspection/index.html
items.how_read: Read on transformer-circuits.pub (re-downloaded; byte-identical to the earlier copy). Read in full: introduction, quick tour, definitions, methods notes, the injected-thoughts set-up, concept extraction, failure modes and layer comparison, and the discussion (recap, limitations, possible mechanisms, implications). Not read: the sections on cross-model comparison, alternative prompts, thoughts vs text, prefill detection and intentional control in detail, and the appendices.
items.finding: Concept vectors (e.g. 'Tell me about {word}' minus a mean over other words) were injected into the residual stream at one layer. Asked whether it notices an injected thought, Opus 4.1 detects and names the concept on 'about 20%' of trials at the best layer (about two thirds of depth) and strength. For all production models, 0 false positives over 100 trials. The models also separate injected 'thoughts' from text, disown or accept prefills depending on earlier activations, and raise or lower the representation of a word they are told to think or not think about. 'In all of our experiments, activations were recorded from and injected into the residual stream at a given layer.' Limits: 'highly unreliable and context-dependent'; one or a few prompt templates; an artificial injection set-up; imperfect concept vectors; an uncontrolled set of models. The metacognitive-representation criterion is 'difficult to do directly, and we do not do so in this work'. Mechanisms are speculative ('multiple different circuits, each of which supports a particular, narrow introspective capability'). Nothing concerns the activation function or gates.
items.bears_on: S2

items.question: A2e: 2025-2026 work on mechanisms and limits of self-monitoring (searched for 2026 work).
items.claim: S2 (self-monitoring could include gates/nonlinearities).
items.citation: U. Macar et al., 'Mechanisms of Introspective Awareness', arXiv 2603.21396v5 (10 Jun 2026); H. Lederman, K. Mahowald, 'Emergent Introspection in AI is Content-Agnostic', arXiv 2603.05414 (Mar 2026); E. Hahami et al., 'Detecting the Disturbance', arXiv 2512.12411 (Dec 2025); E. Ferrara, 'Open-Weight Masked Introspection', arXiv 2608.20569 (Aug 2026); B. Z. Li et al., 'Training Language Models to Explain Their Own Computations', arXiv 2511.08579 (Nov 2025); D. I. Atkinson et al., 'Identifying Introspection From the Inside', arXiv 2610.07186 (Oct 2026); Z. P. Dadfar, arXiv 2602.11358 (Feb 2026).
items.how_read: Macar et al.: abstract plus section 5.3 and the limitations, through text search of the arXiv HTML. All others: abstract only (arXiv abstract pages).
items.finding: Macar et al. (Gemma3-27B with Gemma Scope 2 transcoders) find that MLPs at about 70 % depth are 'causally necessary and sufficient for detection'. 'Evidence carrier' features suppress late 'gate' features. These gates are transcoder features whose decoder pushes toward 'No', not activation-function gates. Ablating the top gates lowers detection from 39.5 % to 10.1 %. They also find the capability emerges from preference optimisation such as DPO, not from SFT. Lederman and Mahowald: detection is content-agnostic anomaly detection. Hahami et al.: in binary detection, global logit shifts explain the apparent accuracy. Localising which of 10 sentences was steered reaches up to 88 % (10 % chance), but only for early-layer injections. Ferrara: 8 open-weight models, interventions on residual-stream sites, attention heads and SAE features. No model's report beats chance (AUROC ≈ 0.5007), while linear probes recover the intervention at 75 % to 95.8 %. Li et al.: fine-tuned 'explainer' models describe features, causal structure and token influence of a model's computation, and work better on themselves than other models do. None of these concerns the model's own activation function.

items.question: A2f: Is there work showing that a network represents its own activation FUNCTION or the state of its own gates/nonlinearities (not residual-stream directions)?
items.claim: S2: 'if the network monitors itself, that is its own activation functions, it may also have a representation of SwiGLU'.
items.citation: Closest analogues: D. Liu et al., 'Attention Schema in Neural Agents', arXiv 2305.17375 (2023); Farrell, Ziman, Graziano, arXiv 2411.00983v3 (2025); Z. Liu et al., 'Deja Vu: Contextual Sparsity for Efficient LLMs at Inference Time', arXiv 2310.17157 (2023).
items.how_read: Liu et al. 2023 and Deja Vu: abstract only. Farrell et al.: as in A1c. Searches listed under not_found.
items.finding: Not found. The closest are 'attention schema' networks, trained with an explicit auxiliary target to predict their own attention scores (the state of a nonlinear selection mechanism). Also close are external predictors (Deja Vu) that predict from a layer's input which attention heads and MLP parameters matter: 'contextual sparsity exists ... it can be accurately predicted'. These are separate small networks, not the model's own representation. Nothing shows a network representing the function silu, ReLU or SwiGLU as such. A gate value silu(g(x)) at the current input is a function of the MLP input by construction, so its decodability from later states says little. Representing the activation function itself would be representing a fixed architectural constant, which no task in these papers requires.
items.bears_on: S2; E4 (description only, as planned); E5

items.question: A3a: Does any work connect self-modelling or self-monitoring with grokking, or activation-level regularisation (UFO-like) with grokking?
items.claim: Implicit in E5 and E5b: a self-monitoring signal might speed generalisation or protect against ungrokking.
items.citation: T. X. Sheppard, A. Albalak, J. Lehman, 'Are UFOs Real? Introducing Unified Factored Organizers', arXiv 2611.11862 (9 Nov 2026); M. A. Kazanskii, 'How to Tame Grokking: Representation Geometry as a Control Signal', arXiv 2607.11666 (Jul 2026); G. L. Howe, 'Structure-Specific Representational Priors Causally Control the Grokking Delay', arXiv 2607.04333 (Jul 2026); X. Zhou, S. Fan, 'NeuralGrok', arXiv 2504.17243 (Apr 2025); D. Doshi et al., 'To grok or not to grok', arXiv 2310.13061 (Oct 2023).
items.how_read: Abstracts only (arXiv abstract pages); web searches.
items.finding: I found no work linking self-modelling or self-prediction with grokking. Activation-level regularisers that change grokking: UFO, a separately trained model of 'regularities in the representations of other networks' that the task network is trained to align with. It cuts steps to grok by 'more than 10x' with weight decay and 'more than 100x' without. GeomDR, a spectral regulariser on the effective dimension of hidden representations, gives up to 52x; 'dimensionality collapse consistently precedes the onset of grokking'. Howe (2026) adds a supervised-contrastive auxiliary loss of identical form but different content. True structure generalises in 22/30 runs, a 'coherent-but-wrong sibling' in 14/15, a random partition in 0/20. A weight-norm-matched control generalises in 0/15, and clamping the weight norm alone gives a median 8.6x speed-up. NeuralGrok trains an auxiliary MLP that transforms gradients (bilevel). Doshi et al. 2023: weight decay, dropout and BatchNorm make networks ignore corrupted labels, and BatchNorm 'de-amplifies the output of memorizing neurons'.
items.bears_on: S1; S2; E5, E5b (Howe's design is a template: same auxiliary loss form with own, other and random targets plus a weight-norm-matched arm; a random-content auxiliary target can block generalisation, so 'othermon' need not be neutral)

items.question: A3b: Target detachment in self-prediction objectives (relevant to selfmon vs selfdet).
items.claim: Plan E5: selfmon (not detached) vs selfdet (detached).
items.citation: Y. Tang et al., 'Understanding Self-Predictive Learning for Reinforcement Learning', arXiv 2212.03319 (2022); X. Chen, K. He, 'Exploring Simple Siamese Representation Learning', arXiv 2011.10566 (2020); J. Teoh et al., 'Next-Latent Prediction Transformers Learn Compact World Models', arXiv 2511.05963v4 (15 Jun 2026).
items.how_read: Tang et al. and SimSiam: abstracts only. NextLat: method passages and limitations, through text search of the arXiv HTML.
items.finding: Tang et al.: in self-predictive learning 'trivial representations (such as constants) minimize the prediction error'. Semi-gradient (stop-gradient) updates and a faster predictor 'are crucial to preventing the representation collapse'. SimSiam: 'collapsing solutions do exist ... a stop-gradient operation plays an essential role in preventing collapsing'. NextLat predicts a transformer's own next latent with stop-gradient on the target, 'used to prevent representational collapse in self-predictive learning'. The next-token loss already grounds it, but 'we empirically observe better performance when applying the stop-gradient'. Premakumar et al. use the full gradient.
items.bears_on: E5 (in selfmon the network can lower the auxiliary loss by making its gate factors low-dimensional or easy to predict. Per-unit batch standardisation removes the scale route but not the dimensional route, so report the effective rank of the gate factors in each arm)

items.question: A3c: Self-modification of weights, and any link to self-monitoring or grokking.
items.claim: User's wider idea of a self-monitoring network.
items.citation: K. Irie, I. Schlag, R. Csordás, J. Schmidhuber, 'A Modern Self-Referential Weight Matrix That Learns to Modify Itself', arXiv 2202.05780 (2022); O. Chang, H. Lipson, 'Neural Network Quine', arXiv 1803.05859 (2018); A. Zweiger et al., 'Self-Adapting Language Models (SEAL)', arXiv 2506.10943 (2025); J. Zhang et al., 'Self-Reference in Large Language Models: The Introspection Threshold for Recursive Self-Improvement', arXiv 2607.04277 (2026).
items.how_read: Abstracts only.
items.finding: SRWM: a weight matrix that rewrites itself with outer products and the delta rule, evaluated on few-shot learning and multi-task RL. Quine: a network trained to output its own weights. It shows a trade-off between replicating itself and classifying MNIST. SEAL: an LLM generates its own fine-tuning data and directives, trained by RL. items.question: C1a: Pehlivan and Williams: the trisector cubic, its coefficients, the linear term, which trisector.
items.claim: Plan S4 and E9.4: the length s of an angle trisector satisfies R s^3 + S s^2 + T = 0 without a linear term.
items.citation: L. Pehlivan, K. S. Williams, 'Angle Trisectors and Cubic Equations', Arhimede Mathematical Journal 13(1), Spring 2026, pp. 11-31 (local copy <root>/amj/amj.txt and amj.pdf).
items.how_read: Full article in the local text copy. Journal pages 14 and 16 checked against the rendered PDF.
items.finding: Notation: a = |BC|, b = |CA|, c = |AB|, θ = C/3. P and Q lie on BA in the order B, P, Q, A, with angle BCP = PCQ = QCA = θ. There are two trisectors: r = |CP| (next to side CB) and s = |CQ| (next to side CA). Theorem 1: s is a positive root of R x^3 + S x^2 + T = 0 with R = a^2 c^2 − (a^2 − b^2)^2, S = 3 a b^2 c^2 and T = −a b^2 (a+b+c)(a+b−c)(a−b+c)(−a+b+c) = −a b^2 V. Article: 'we find amazingly that the coefficients of s^6, s^5, s^4 and s are all 0'. So there is no linear term, and the quadratic term is present (S > 0). Also T < 0, and R can have either sign or be 0. Theorem 2: r satisfies the same form with a and b swapped: R' = b^2 c^2 − (a^2 − b^2)^2, S' = 3 a^2 b c^2, T' = −a^2 b V. 'Cubic equations cannot be avoided': R and R' cannot both vanish.
items.bears_on: S4; E9.4; users_premises 3

items.question: C1b: Steps of the derivation.
items.claim: Plan S4: 'derived by nesting the angle-bisector theorem twice and using cos 3θ = 4cos^3 θ − 3cos θ'.
items.citation: Pehlivan and Williams 2026, sections 1 and 2.
items.how_read: Full text. The step after (12) was checked symbolically with sympy and numerically (scripts in <root>/act_review/lit_self/scripts/).
items.finding: (i) Bisector length formula l^2 = ab(1 − c^2/(a+b)^2) and the bisector ratio (2), (3). (ii) These are applied to the two overlapping triangles CBQ, whose angle at C is bisected by CP, and CPA, bisected by CQ, giving (4) to (8). Each trisector bisects the angle between the other trisector and a side, so 'twice on two overlapping sub-triangles' is more exact than 'nested'. (iii) w = r/s solves (a+s)b w^2 − a s w − ab = 0, so w = (as + E)/(2(a+s)b) with E^2 = a^2 s^2 + 4ab^2 s + 4a^2 b^2. (iv) The cosine rule in triangle BCP gives cos θ = (as + E)/(4ab). (v) 4cos^3 θ − 3cos θ = cos 3θ = cos C = (a^2 + b^2 − c^2)/(2ab) gives (12): (−2ab^2 + b^2 s + a s^2) E = 2ab^2(a^2 + b^2 − c^2) − 3ab^2 s^2 − a^2 s^3. (vi) Squaring and expanding (with MAPLE) leaves 4ab^2 (R s^3 + S s^2 + T). The printed squared equation has a typo: it reads (a^2 s^2 + 4ab^2 s^2 + 4a^2 b^2) where (9) has 4ab^2 s. I checked symbolically that only (9) gives exactly 4ab^2(R s^3 + S s^2 + T); the typo version leaves every power from s^0 to s^6. The theorem is unaffected. The article also contains minor slips: Example 5 cites 'Theorem 7' for formula (34), which is Theorem 8, and section 5 is titled 'Relationship between r and r'.
items.bears_on: S4; E9

items.question: C1c: Roots, root selection, and the quadratic case.
items.claim: E9: properties of the trisector cubic.
items.citation: Pehlivan and Williams 2026, sections 2 to 5 (Theorems 3 to 8, Examples 1 to 5).
items.how_read: Full text. All five examples recomputed numerically.
items.finding: Discriminant: Δ = −4S^3 T − 27 R^2 T^2 = −27 a b^2 T W^2 ≥ 0 with W = a^2 c^4 − (2a^4 − a^2 b^2 − b^4) c^2 + (a^2 − b^2)^3. So for R ≠ 0 the cubic always has three real roots, two of them equal when W = 0. If R > 0 there is exactly one positive root, and it is s (Theorem 5); the same holds for W = 0 (Theorem 6). If R < 0 there are two positive roots, and the choice uses λ = sin(C/3) (Theorem 7). R = 0 exactly when 2A = B or 2A = B + π. The equation is then quadratic, with s = (b/a) sqrt((4a^2 − b^2)/3) (Theorem 3), and Theorem 4 gives r. For example, in the 4-5-6 triangle s = sqrt(21) and r = (9 sqrt(21) − 21)/5. Theorem 8 (W ≠ 0): r = (abs/(a+s)) (a^2 + b^2 − c^2 − as − s^2)/(−2ab^2 + b^2 s + a s^2). All examples reproduce: s = 4.5825757, 3.1828343, 7, 1.4836776 and 0.98536794; r = 4.0486363 and 1.19486333.
items.bears_on: S4; E9

items.question: C1d: Closed formulas in angles, and the trisection cubic inside the article.
items.claim: S4: the link to trisection.
items.citation: Pehlivan and Williams 2026, section 4 (equation (32), property (33), formula for s); they cite Trisna, Mashadi, Gemawati, IOSR J. Math. 16(5) (2020), Theorem 3.1, for s = b sin A / sin(A + θ).
items.how_read: Full text. Formulas checked numerically on 20,000 random triangles.
items.finding: s = b sin A / sin(A + θ), from the sine rule in triangle QCA (by symmetry r = a sin B / sin(B + θ)). In sides: s = b sqrt(V) / ((b^2 + c^2 − a^2) λ + sqrt((1 − λ^2) V)), where λ = sin(C/3) is a root of x^3 − (3/4) x + sqrt(V)/(8ab) = 0. Since sqrt(V)/(2ab) = sin C, this is 4x^3 − 3x + sin C = 0, the classical trisection cubic (depressed). Its roots are sin θ and (−sin θ ± sqrt(3) cos θ)/2; λ is the smaller positive root if c^2 < a^2 + b^2, the larger if c^2 > a^2 + b^2, and 1/2 if C = π/2. For R = 0 the article also gives r = s sqrt(3) / (2 sin(π/3 + A)) when 2A = B.

items.question: C1e: Own checks: the depressed form and the triple-angle form of the trisector cubic (not in the article).
items.claim: Plan E9.4: 'in w = 1/s it reads T w^3 + S w + R = 0: already depressed'.
items.citation: Own computation from Pehlivan and Williams' Theorem 1; scripts trisector_check.py, trisector_angle_form.py and amj_expand_check.py in <root>/act_review/lit_self/scripts/
items.how_read: sympy expansion; numerical check on 20,000 random triangles (worst relative residual 1.5e-13 for Theorems 1 and 2).
items.finding: Confirmed: in w = 1/s the equation is T w^3 + S w + R = 0, with no w^2 term (residual about 1e-16 on the examples). Stronger: with σ = h_c/s, where h_c = sqrt(V)/(2c) = b sin A is the altitude from C, the normalised cubic is σ^3 − (3/4)σ + const = 0 (sympy). Numerically it is 4σ^3 − 3σ + sin(3A + C) = 0, with σ = sin(A + C/3) (max error 8e-13); in addition R sqrt(V)/(2ab^2c^3) = sin(2A − B) = −sin(3A + C). So finding the trisector length means trisecting the angle 3A + C = π + 2A − B. The cubic is the sine form of the triple-angle (Chebyshev) identity, and the missing linear term in s is the missing quadratic term in 1/s. Viète's trigonometric solution of a cubic with three real roots was also checked numerically: the roots are −p/3 + 2U cos(φ − 2πk/3) with cos 3φ = −Q/(2U^3), max error 2e-9 over 100,000 random cubics.

items.question: C2a: Products of trigonometric features in grokking (Nanda et al.), and use of the words bisection or trisection.
items.claim: S3/S4: quadratic units and multiple-angle identities.
items.citation: N. Nanda, L. Chan, T. Lieberum, J. Smith, J. Steinhardt, 'Progress measures for grokking via mechanistic interpretability', ICLR 2023, arXiv 2301.05217.
items.how_read: PDF text: sections 3 and 4 read; whole text searched for terms.
items.finding: The algorithm computes cos(w(a+b)) and sin(w(a+b)) 'using the trigonometric identities' with products cos(wa)cos(wb) and sin(wa)sin(wb): 'In our networks, this is computed in the attention and MLP layers.' Then cos(w(a+b−c)) is formed linearly in the unembedding. 'Two of the attention heads approximately compute degree-2 polynomials of sines and cosines of a particular frequency.' 'Most neurons are also well-approximated by degree-2 polynomials': 433 of 512 neurons (84.6 %) have over 85 % of their variance explained by a single frequency (the model's MLP uses ReLU). The words bisection, trisection, half-angle, double-angle, triple-angle and Chebyshev do not occur.
items.bears_on: S3 (products, i.e. quadratic terms, are what the network must build; with ReLU it approximates them); E1 and E6 (the bilinear arm provides products natively)

items.question: C2b: Clock vs Pizza (Zhong et al.): role of products, halving and doubling of angles.
items.citation: Z. Zhong, Z. Liu, M. Tegmark, J. Andreas, 'The Clock and the Pizza: Two Stories in Mechanistic Explanation of Neural Networks', NeurIPS 2023, arXiv 2306.17844.
items.how_read: PDF text: sections 2 and 3 and appendix A read; whole text searched for terms.
items.finding: Clock logits are Q = (E_a,x E_b,x − E_a,y E_b,y) E_c,x + (E_a,x E_b,y + E_a,y E_b,x) E_c,y, which are products. 'Crucial to this algorithm is the fact that the attention mechanism can be leveraged to perform multiplication.' Pizza first averages the embeddings: E_ab = (E_a + E_b)/2 = cos(w(a−b)/2) (cos(w(a+b)/2), sin(w(a+b)/2)), a vector along the half-sum angle. It then turns this into |cos(w(a−b)/2)| (cos(w(a+b)), sin(w(a+b))) by doubling the angle with absolute values: '|cos(t)| − |sin(t)| is approximately cos(2t)'. 'Clock requires multiplication of inputs in Step 2, while Pizza requires only absolute value computation, which is easily implemented by the ReLU layers. If neural networks lack inductive biases toward implementing multiplication, they may be more likely to implement Pizza.' The words bisection and trisection do not occur, although the averaging step amounts to taking the angle bisector (my reading).
items.bears_on: S3; S4 (bisection appears in substance, not in name); E1, E2, E6 (the nonlinearity that supplies or lacks products changes the algorithm)

items.question: C2c: Quadratic and power activations in grokking (Gromov; Doshi et al.).
items.claim: S3: SwiGLU is roughly quadratic, so results for quadratic units carry over.
items.citation: A. Gromov, 'Grokking modular arithmetic', arXiv 2301.02679 (2023); D. Doshi, T. He, A. Das, A. Gromov, 'Grokking Modular Polynomials', arXiv 2406.03495 (2024).
items.how_read: Gromov: section 2 and appendices A and B read in the PDF text. Doshi et al.: section 2 and appendix B read; rest not read.
items.finding: Gromov: two-layer MLP; 'in the case of quadratic activation the full network function takes an even simpler form f(x) = (1/DN) W^(2) (W^(1) x)^2 ... cubic in parameters and quadratic in its inputs'. Squaring the summed phasors of n and m gives the cross term 2 e^{2πik(n+m)/p}, the angle sum, plus doubled-angle terms in 2n and 2m that cancel in the readout. The same weights also work with ReLU but need more width ('only mildly sensitive to the choice of activation function'). Doshi et al.: for S-term sums they use φ(x) = x^S, and 'Since S = 3 in all the examples, we use cubic (φ(x) = x^3) activation function'. The S-fold product supplies the S-term angle sum. Words bisection, trisection, triple-angle and Chebyshev: not used.
items.bears_on: S3; E6, E7, E9.5 (degree of the unit sets which multiple-angle products are available; a bilinear unit gives degree 2, two stacked give up to 4)

items.question: C2d: Networks that solve cubic equations, trisect angles, or use Cardano or Viète; interpretability of such methods.
items.claim: S3/S4: networks might find Cardano's substitution or trisection.
items.citation: R. Thomas, M. Bani-Yaghoub, 'On the Limits of Interpretable Machine Learning in Quintic Root Classification', arXiv 2602.23467 (Feb 2026); E. Shaska, T. Shaska, 'Galois groups of polynomials and neurosymbolic networks', arXiv 2501.12978 (Jan 2025).
items.how_read: Abstracts only; web searches (queries in not_found).
items.finding: Apart from Bottazzi's post, I found no study of a network that learns to solve cubics by Cardano or Viète or to trisect angles. Thomas and Bani-Yaghoub classify real-root configurations of polynomials up to degree 5. Neural networks reach 84.3 % balanced accuracy on quintics from raw coefficients, and decision trees match them (84.2 %) only when given a sign-change-at-critical-points feature. They find 'no evidence that the evaluated ML models autonomously recover discrete, human-interpretable mathematical rules'; the networks learn 'continuous, data-dependent geometric approximations'. Shaska and Shaska build a neurosymbolic network to classify Galois groups.
items.bears_on: S3; S4

users_premises.premise: A network that monitors its own activations has a representation of its activation function.
users_premises.detail: None of the sources I read shows this, and none attempts it. Ji-An et al. (residual-stream directions only, 'exclusively on the residual stream'), Lindsey (residual-stream injections), Binder et al. (behaviour) and the 2025-2026 follow-ups concern directions, features or behaviour. Even the monitoring of residual-stream directions is contested: Singh, Linzen and Ravfogel 2026 explain the Ji-An results by input features and the Lindsey-style results by generic anomaly detection, and Ferrara 2026 finds no open-weight model above chance. The 'gate' features in Macar et al. 2026 are transcoder features, not GLU gates. The closest analogue is a network trained with an explicit auxiliary target to predict its own attention scores (attention schema). Gate values at the current input are functions of the MLP input by construction, so their decodability (E4) would not show a representation of the function SwiGLU.

users_premises.premise: The Wolfram post's network and results are as README 8.7 describes them.
users_premises.detail: Wrong: the network is 3-64-64-64-15-1 with ReLU, not four layers of 15. The activation function is named (ReLU, code Ramp). The notebook with all code is linked from the post, and the trained net and SAE weights are downloadable. '15x15x15x15' refers only to the 49 single-polynomial networks at the end. Overstated: the nine features were picked by eye, and they 'depend only on t' at R^2 0.88 to 0.985. Their b-invariance rests on a visual comparison at b = 0 and b = 1. Correct: inputs in [−3, 3]; SAE with 64 features, top-4, on the last hidden layer (standardised post-ReLU activations, R^2 0.996); c between 0.175 and 0.35, median 0.30; scaling the features stretches the curve vertically; one network, one SAE. The README's countercheck with '15 own networks of the same size' did not use the post's size.

users_premises.premise: The trisector cubic has no linear term.
users_premises.detail: Theorem 1 of Pehlivan and Williams: the trisector CQ (next to side CA) has length s, a positive root of R s^3 + S s^2 + T = 0 with R = a^2c^2 − (a^2 − b^2)^2, S = 3ab^2c^2, T = −ab^2(a+b+c)(a+b−c)(a−b+c)(−a+b+c). The coefficients of s^6, s^5, s^4 and s vanish. I verified this symbolically and on 20,000 random triangles; the printed squared equation has a typo (s^2 for s) that does not affect it. The other trisector satisfies the same form with a and b swapped. Caveats: for 2A = B or 2A = B + π, R = 0 and the equation is quadratic. With R < 0 there are two positive roots, and the right one is chosen with λ = sin(C/3). The missing linear term makes the equation in 1/s depressed. Substituting σ = h_c/s gives exactly the sine triple-angle equation 4σ^3 − 3σ + sin(3A + C) = 0 (my derivation, verified).
